marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q001.takeaway: Terminal sulcus separates oral anterior two-thirds from pharyngeal posterior one-third.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q001.displayText:
The anterior two-thirds of the tongue is demarcated from the posterior one-third by the terminal sulcus, also known as the sulcus terminalis.

Sulcus terminalis divides the tongue into anterior and posterior parts. The anterior or oral part faces superiorly and the posterior or pharyngeal part faces posteriorly.

Sigmoid sulcus is present on the mastoid surface of the temporal bone. Gingival sulcus is present between a tooth and the surrounding gingival tissue. Median sulcus is the central sulcus present on the tongue.

rationales.a: Sigmoid sulcus is a temporal-bone mastoid landmark, not the tongue boundary.
rationales.b: Gingival sulcus lies between tooth and gingiva.
rationales.d: Median sulcus runs along the midline dorsum; terminal sulcus separates anterior oral and posterior pharyngeal tongue.

marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q002.takeaway: Foliate papillae are leaf-like folds on posterolateral tongue, near terminal sulcus.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q002.displayText:
The structure marked A shows the foliate papillae, which lie bilaterally on either side of the tongue near the sulcus terminalis.

Filiform papillae are minute cylindrical or conical projections mainly on the dorsal anterior two-thirds. Fungiform papillae are large, rounded, red papillae mainly on the lingual margins and dorsal surface. Foliate papillae are red, leaf-like mucosal ridges present bilaterally near the sulcus terminalis. Circumvallate papillae are large cylindrical structures, around 8-12 in number, arranged in a V-shaped row immediately anterior to the sulcus terminalis.

rationales.a: Filiform papillae are conical, numerous and mechanical, not the red leaf-like folds at lateral tongue.
rationales.b: Fungiform papillae are rounded/red and scattered along margins, not leaf-like bilateral folds near terminal sulcus.
rationales.d: Circumvallate papillae are large posterior V-shaped papillae anterior to terminal sulcus, not lateral leaf-like folds.

marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q003.takeaway: Palatoglossus is a pharyngeal-arch muscle, unlike other tongue muscles derived from occipital myotomes.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q003.displayText:
All the muscles of the tongue are derived from occipital myotomes except palatoglossus. Palatoglossus is derived from the fourth pharyngeal arch.

Accordingly, all tongue muscles are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus, which is supplied through the pharyngeal plexus.

rationales.a: Genioglossus is an intrinsic/extrinsic tongue muscle derived from occipital myotomes and supplied by XII.
rationales.c: Styloglossus is also an occipital-myotome muscle and is supplied by XII.
rationales.d: Superior longitudinal muscle is intrinsic tongue musculature with hypoglossal supply.

marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q004.takeaway: Left genioglossus paresis makes protruded tongue deviate toward left.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q004.displayText:
The image shows deviation of the tongue to the left; the left genioglossus is paralyzed.

When both genioglossi contract they protrude the anterior tongue in the midline. When one contracts, it protrudes and pushes the tongue to the opposite side. Genioglossus also depresses the central tongue and is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve.

With hypoglossal nerve palsy, the ipsilateral genioglossus is paralyzed and the protruded tongue deviates toward the affected side because of unopposed contraction on the normal side.

Genioglossus is attached to the genial tubercle and helps prevent the tongue from falling backward and obstructing respiration; the source notes this as the safety muscle of the tongue.
emphasis: deviation of the tongue to the left
pushes the tongue to the opposite side

rationales.a: Styloglossus retracts/elevates tongue and is not the unilateral protrusion muscle whose paralysis matches ipsilateral deviation.
rationales.b: Right styloglossus does not explain tongue deviation toward the left when protruded.
rationales.c: Right genioglossus weakness would cause deviation to the right, opposite observed.

marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q005.takeaway: Chorda tympani carries taste from anterior two-thirds; lingual nerve carries general sensation.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q005.displayText:
The clinical picture indicates facial nerve damage above the stylomastoid foramen with involvement of the chorda tympani.

Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by chorda tympani, whereas general sensation is carried by the lingual nerve.

rationales.a: Glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste from posterior third, not anterior two-thirds.
rationales.c: Hypoglossal is motor to tongue muscles and carries no taste.
rationales.d: Lingual nerve carries general sensation from anterior tongue; taste fibers travel with chorda tympani.

marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q006.takeaway: Glossopharyngeal nerve supplies taste to circumvallate papillae despite their anterior position.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q006.displayText:
Taste from the circumvallate papillae is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, except the circumvallate papillae, is carried by chorda tympani. Glossopharyngeal innervation includes the circumvallate papillae, posterior one-third of the tongue, palatoglossal arches, and oropharynx.

Taste buds in the extreme posterior tongue and epiglottis receive fibres from the internal laryngeal branch of the vagus.

rationales.a: Chorda tympani carries taste from anterior two-thirds except circumvallate papillae.
rationales.b: Greater petrosal nerve carries palatal taste/parasympathetic fibers, not circumvallate tongue taste.
rationales.c: Internal laryngeal nerve carries sensation/taste from epiglottic region, not circumvallate papillae.

marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q007.takeaway: Lingual nerve (V3) carries pain from tongue tip.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q007.displayText: Pain sensation at the tip of the tongue is carried by the lingual nerve, which is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.

rationales.a: Glossopharyngeal supplies posterior third of tongue; the ulcer is at tip in anterior territory.
rationales.b: Chorda tympani carries taste, while pain/general sensation from anterior tongue travels through lingual nerve.
rationales.d: Vagus supplies epiglottis/laryngopharynx, not tongue tip.

marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q008.takeaway: Tip-of-tongue lymph drains first to submental nodes.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q008.displayText:
The submental lymph node is biopsied first because it is the sentinel node for lesions at the tip of the tongue.

In squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue, submental nodes are involved in lesions of the tip, whereas submandibular nodes are involved in lesions of the lateral tongue. Bilateral neck-node spread is common because lymphatic vessels cross the midline.

rationales.a: Submandibular nodes are first for lateral tongue lesions, not the tip in the described case.
rationales.c: Deep cervical nodes receive downstream drainage after initial submental nodes.
rationales.d: Jugulo-omohyoid is a deep cervical node receiving later tongue drainage, not first sentinel for tip.

marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q009.takeaway: Marginal anterior-tongue lesion drains first to ipsilateral submandibular nodes.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q009.displayText:
The image shows carcinoma involving the marginal part of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Lymphatics from this region drain first to unilateral submandibular lymph nodes.

All lymphatics from the tongue ultimately drain into deep cervical nodes along the internal jugular vein; the jugulo-omohyoid nodes are therefore described as lymph nodes of the tongue.
emphasis: marginal part of the anterior two-thirds

rationales.a: Submental nodes chiefly receive tip/central lower lip drainage; marginal anterior lateral tongue first reaches ipsilateral submandibular nodes.
rationales.b: Deep cervical nodes receive subsequent drainage from the tongue, not first regional nodes.
rationales.c: The source specifies unilateral first-echelon submandibular drainage from the marginal anterior tongue; bilateral spread is more characteristic of midline lesions.

marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q010.takeaway: Hypoglossal is motor only, not a sensory nerve to palate.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q010.displayText:
The image shows a cleft palate. Sensory supply to the palate is not provided by the hypoglossal nerve, which is a pure motor nerve.

General sensation from most of the soft palate is carried by the lesser palatine nerve (V2), pharyngeal branches of the glossopharyngeal nerve, and the plexus around the tonsil. Taste from the oral surface of the soft palate is carried by the lesser palatine nerve; taste fibres initially travel in the greater petrosal nerve, a branch of the facial nerve, and traverse the pterygopalatine ganglion without synapsing.

All muscles of the soft palate are supplied through the pharyngeal plexus (CN X) except tensor veli palatini, which is supplied by the mandibular nerve. The hard palate is supplied by the greater palatine and nasopalatine branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion.

rationales.a: Facial nerve contributes taste via chorda tympani and parasympathetic palatal supply; it does supply palate.
rationales.c: Glossopharyngeal nerve contributes palatal sensation via pharyngeal/tonsillar plexuses.
rationales.d: Maxillary division provides sensory palatal innervation through greater/lesser palatine branches; hypoglossal is the pure motor nerve.

marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q011.takeaway: Palatine branches of V2 carry palatal sensation; taste afferents ultimately reach VII via greater petrosal route.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q011.displayText:
The sensory fibres from taste buds in the hard and soft palate travel along the trigeminal nerve.

Taste from the oral surface of the soft palate is carried by the lesser palatine nerve. The taste fibres initially travel in the greater petrosal nerve, a branch of the facial nerve, and pass through the pterygopalatine ganglion without synapsing.

rationales.a: Facial nerve carries taste centrally, but palatine branches of V2 carry fibers from palate per source peripheral route; the answer refers to that route.
rationales.c: Glossopharyngeal carries taste from posterior tongue/oropharynx, not palatal taste pathway.
rationales.d: Vagus carries taste from epiglottis, not hard/soft palate.

reconstruction.sourceProblem: The source first keys palatal taste sensation to trigeminal nerve but then describes taste fibers traveling in greater petrosal nerve (facial nerve), conflating peripheral carriage in V2 palatine branches with the cranial taste afferent route.
reconstruction.reconstructedContent:
The sensory fibres from taste buds in the hard and soft palate travel along the trigeminal nerve.

Taste from the oral surface of the soft palate is carried by the lesser palatine nerve. The taste fibres initially travel in the greater petrosal nerve, a branch of the facial nerve, and pass through the pterygopalatine ganglion without synapsing. Clarification: palatine branches of V2 convey sensory fibers from palate peripherally; taste afferents then travel centrally through greater petrosal nerve of CN VII, passing pterygopalatine ganglion without synapsing. The source key “trigeminal nerve” refers to peripheral palatine nerve carriage, not the central taste modality pathway.
reconstruction.evidenceBasis: Source explanation and key for Anatomy ED8 q11; text itself names both trigeminal palatine route and greater petrosal nerve. No key or source gate altered.
reconstruction.reviewNote: Completed terminology clarification; V2 route is retained as the source-keyed peripheral carrier, while CN VII is identified as the central taste afferent pathway.

marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q012.takeaway: Tonsillar branch of facial artery supplies tonsil rather than palate.
marrow__ANAT_CH32_Q012.displayText:
The tonsillar branch of the facial artery supplies the palatine tonsil and not the palate.

The hard palate is supplied by the greater (descending) palatine artery, a branch of the third part of the maxillary artery. The soft palate is supplied by the ascending palatine branch of the facial artery, the ascending pharyngeal artery, and lesser palatine arteries.
emphasis: tonsillar branch of the facial artery

rationales.b: Ascending palatine artery is a facial artery branch supplying soft palate.
rationales.c: Descending/greater and lesser palatine arteries supply hard and soft palate from maxillary artery.
rationales.d: Ascending pharyngeal artery contributes to soft-palate supply; the tonsillar facial branch is directed to palatine tonsil.
